nameStory: This tiny freshwater copepod is named after Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld, a famous Finnish-Swedish Arctic explorer who led the first successful navigation of the Northeast Passage in the 1870s. The genus name Attheyella honors Thomas Atthey, a 19th-century British naturalist who studied microscopic marine life.
description: Attheyella nordenskioldii is a microscopic freshwater crustacean called a copepod that you'll need a magnifying glass or microscope to truly see. These tiny creatures are smaller than a pinhead, typically measuring only about 0.5-1 millimeter long. They have a teardrop-shaped body with a distinct head section and long, feathery antennae that they use like oars to paddle through the water. Their bodies are usually translucent to pale whitish, making them nearly invisible in water samples.

idTips.label: Body shape and size
idTips.description: Extremely small teardrop-shaped body less than 1mm long, visible as a tiny moving speck in water samples

idTips.label: Swimming antennae
idTips.description: Two prominent feathery antennae that beat rhythmically like tiny oars, creating jerky swimming movements

idTips.label: Transparent appearance
idTips.description: Nearly colorless, translucent body that appears like a moving glass bead in pond water

idTips.label: Segmented body
idTips.description: Body clearly divided into sections with a broader front portion and narrower tail-like rear section

idTips.label: Habitat preference
idTips.description: Found in shallow, vegetated areas of ponds and slow streams where organic matter accumulates

habitat: This species lives in shallow freshwater environments throughout New England, particularly in small ponds, marshes, and the quiet edges of slow-moving streams. Look for them in areas with aquatic vegetation where decaying plant matter provides food sources. They prefer habitats with soft sediments and are often found among submerged leaves and plant debris.

seasonality.spring: Active as water temperatures rise, with populations beginning to increase as ice melts and organic matter becomes available.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when populations are highest and most easily observed in warm, productive waters.
seasonality.fall: Still active but populations may decline as temperatures drop and food sources become less abundant.
seasonality.winter: Present but less active in unfrozen water bodies, though difficult to observe due to reduced movement.

funFact: Despite being smaller than the period at the end of this sentence, these microscopic creatures can live for several months and are incredibly important recyclers - a single pond may contain millions of them working together to break down dead plant material and keep the ecosystem healthy.
confusionNotes: Easily confused with other microscopic copepods in the same family, which all look like tiny swimming specks to the naked eye. The only reliable way to distinguish this species is through microscopic examination of specific anatomical features like antenna structure and leg arrangements.
contextualKnowledge: Copepods are among the most abundant animals on Earth, though most people have never heard of them because they're too small to see without magnification. The name 'copepod' means 'oar-foot' in Greek, referring to their paddle-like swimming appendages.
compareHints: **Note: Information about distinguishing features from related species should be considered uncertain due to limited reference material.** This species likely differs from other Canthocamptidae family members in subtle details of antenna segmentation and swimming appendage structure. Without other Attheyella species in New England, comparison with similar genera would require microscopic examination of mouthparts and leg characteristics that aren't visible in field observations.
